summary.text: Velocity is a vector: it combines how fast an object moves with the direction it moves in.
Its size alone is speed, so '5 metres per second' is just a speed, while '5 metres per second east' is a velocity.
Because velocity includes direction, an object that changes speed, direction or both is accelerating, even when its speed stays steady.

facts.label: Unit
facts.value: Metres per second (m/s) in the SI system

facts.label: Scalar part
facts.value: Speed is the magnitude of the velocity vector

facts.label: Escape velocity
facts.value: About 11,200 m/s from Earth's surface, in any direction

facts.label: Average velocity
facts.value: Change in position divided by the duration, Δs/Δt

items.prompt: A weather report says wind is blowing at 20 kilometres per hour. A pilot needs to know the wind velocity. What is missing?

options.label: The wind's temperature
The wind's mass
The wind's direction
The wind's pressure

items.explain: Velocity needs both magnitude and direction; a speed alone is only the magnitude.

items.prompt: Two joggers each run at 4 metres per second, one north and one south. Which statement is correct?

options.label: They have the same speed but different velocities
They have different speeds and the same velocity
They have the same speed and the same velocity
They have different speeds and different velocities

items.explain: Speed is the magnitude only, so both share it, but velocity includes direction, which differs.

items.prompt: A car circles a track at a steady 20 kilometres per hour. Is it accelerating?

options.label: No, because its speed never changes
No, because it ends up near where it started
Yes, because its speed is low
Yes, because its direction keeps changing

items.explain: Constant speed in a changing direction is not constant velocity, so the car is accelerating.

items.prompt: What does an object need to have a constant velocity?

options.label: Constant speed in a constant direction, a straight line
Constant speed along any path, even a curve
Constant direction while speeding up steadily
Constant distance covered every minute

items.explain: Constant velocity means constant speed in a constant direction, which forces a straight path.

items.prompt: On a displacement-time graph, what does the steepness of a line touching the curve at one point show?

options.label: Total distance travelled so far
The object's mass at that moment
Kinetic energy at that moment
The instantaneous velocity at that moment

items.explain: Instantaneous velocity is the slope of the tangent line to the displacement-time curve at that point.

items.prompt: A hiker walks 3 km out and 3 km back to the start. How do average speed and average velocity compare?

options.label: Both are the same, because the path was the same
Average velocity is smaller, since displacement ends at zero
Average velocity is larger, since it counts direction
Neither can be found without knowing mass

items.explain: Average velocity is never greater than average speed, because distance only grows while displacement can shrink or change direction.

paragraphs.heading: Size and direction
paragraphs.text: Velocity measures speed in a particular direction of motion. That makes it a vector quantity: both a size, called its magnitude, and a direction are needed to define it. Strip away the direction and the magnitude left over is speed, measured in metres per second in the SI system.

paragraphs.heading: Scalar or vector
paragraphs.text: A simple example shows the difference. "5 metres per second" is a scalar, while "5 metres per second east" is a vector. Everyday speech often treats speed and velocity as the same, but in physics speed tells only how fast, while velocity adds the direction.

paragraphs.heading: Turning counts as accelerating
paragraphs.text: Because velocity carries direction, a change of direction is a change of velocity. Any change in speed, direction or both is called acceleration. Constant velocity needs a steady speed in a fixed direction, which means straight-line motion. A car going round a circle at a constant 20 kilometres per hour has a steady speed but a changing velocity, so it is accelerating.

paragraphs.heading: Writing the parts
paragraphs.text: A velocity vector can be broken into Cartesian components, one along each of the x-, y- and z-axes. Some textbooks label these components with subscripts. Others name them u, v and w.

paragraphs.heading: Quantities built on it
paragraphs.text: Several other quantities are built from velocity. Momentum, p, is mass times velocity, 𝒑 = m𝒗, and is a vector. Kinetic energy, Eₖ = 1/2mv², is a scalar, since it depends on the square of the velocity. Leaving Earth from its surface takes an escape velocity of about 11 200 m/s, whichever way the object heads, so it is really a speed, and "escape speed" would be the better name.
